title: Zephyrine and the Room
premise: Quentin Marchetti, a hospice nurse who hears the dying count backwards from ten and has built a career on not believing, returns to their grandmother's shuttered house to settle the estate and discovers that every photograph taken inside it now contains an extra wooden chair — a chair that, in the oldest pictures, is empty, but in the recent ones is not. The house is a half-finished summoning, begun by the town's founders, that harvests memory to feed something that waits beneath the frost; the backwards counting is the dying being pulled through it early. As winter closes in, Quentin, their estranged sister Odette, and the last living founder's descendant must complete or break the ritual, learning that the chair's occupant is a version of Quentin who stayed and believed. In the end, Quentin chooses to sit in the chair themselves, trading their memories of love for the town's release — and the final chapter belongs to Odette, who remembers everything and must decide whether a person is their memories or their love.
about_author: Juniper Almeida is the pen name of a former palliative-care volunteer who spent three years listening to the last words of strangers and writing them down. Zephyrine and the Room is their second novel, written in a rented farmhouse where, they insist, nothing unusual ever happened.

chapters.title: The Count
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. At the hospice, Mrs. Halloran counts backwards from ten and dies mid-four, and Quentin notes it as the eleventh patient to do so, refusing the pattern a name. The emotional beat is professional detachment curdling into unease; Quentin's disbelief is established as a discipline, not a conclusion.

chapters.title: Probate Weather
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. A lawyer's letter sends Quentin back to the hometown of Zephyrine to empty their grandmother's house; Odette refuses to come, citing what happened 'the last time.' The beat is dread disguised as errand-running, with the frost already unnaturally thick on the town.

chapters.title: Everything in Its Place, Plus One
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Sorting boxes of photographs, Quentin finds the extra chair in every interior shot — including pictures taken that morning, where the chair sits closer than in yesterday's. The beat is the first hard crack in disbelief: Quentin burns one photo and the smell of scorched wood fills the whole house.

chapters.title: Odette at the Door
chapters.summary: Odette's POV. Odette arrives unannounced at midnight, unable to stay away, and the siblings' old wound — their mother's death in this house — surfaces as accusation. The beat is love expressed as blame; Odette admits she stopped believing too, but only after believing too much.

chapters.title: What the Founders Buried
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. In the town archive, Quentin reads the founders' ledger: a covenant ritual begun in 1897, left unfinished, its final page cut out. The beat is the horror of bureaucratic evil — the ritual has a budget, a roster, and Quentin's grandmother's name on the last line.

chapters.title: The Chair in the Kitchen
chapters.summary: Odette's POV. The chair appears physically in the kitchen overnight, oak and wrong, and neither sibling can touch it without hearing a name whispered in their mother's voice. The beat is terror turning domestic; they eat dinner facing away from it.

chapters.title: Ten, Nine, Eight
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. A neighbor, Mr. Ives, begins counting backwards on his porch, days before any illness, and Quentin sits with him through the numbers, learning each count takes a memory from the town — the school, the river, a wedding. The beat is grief for strangers.

chapters.title: Zephyrine
chapters.summary: Odette's POV. Odette finds grandmother's journals: Zephyrine was a ritual-keeper who tried to finish the founders' work alone and instead trapped the thing halfway, buying the town a century. The beat is posthumous reconciliation — the grandmother they resented was a warden, not a witch.

chapters.title: The Frost Writes
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Frost patterns on the windows begin forming script — the missing final page, writing itself as the ritual nears completion. Quentin photographs it; in the photos, the chair now has an occupant with Quentin's posture. The beat is recognition without acceptance.

chapters.title: The Last Founder
chapters.summary: Third person limited on Elias Voss, elderly descendant of the founders, who has kept his family's half of the covenant in a locked smokehouse. He tells them the ritual needs three: a keeper, a believer, and a sacrifice. The beat is reluctant alliance; Voss has spent his life preparing to be the sacrifice and resents the company.

chapters.title: What Happened the Last Time
chapters.summary: Odette's POV. The truth of their mother's death emerges: she sat in the chair for one night to buy Zephyrine time, and came out with no memory of her children. Odette has hated Quentin for forgetting to grieve; Quentin has hated Odette for remembering too loudly. The beat is the theme of memory made flesh.

chapters.title: Seven, Six
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Mr. Ives reaches six and forgets his wife's face; half the town has stopped attending church because they can't recall why. Quentin, still insisting this is mass hysteria, begins keeping a written list of everything they love — just in case. The beat is disbelief becoming a liability.

chapters.title: The Room Behind the Pantry
chapters.summary: Odette's POV. Behind a false pantry wall they find the original ritual room: a circle of thirteen chairs, twelve rotted to dust, and Zephyrine's chair — the thirteenth — pristine, facing a door that was bricked shut from the inside. The beat is claustrophobic revelation.

chapters.title: Five
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Voss begins his own countdown, having chosen his night; he explains the mechanics — the thing beneath the frost eats memory, and the ritual doesn't banish it but feeds it a finished life, whole, so it sleeps for another century. The beat is moral horror: salvation as an edible person.

chapters.title: The Photographs Turn
chapters.summary: Odette's POV. All the photographs now show the chair occupied, and the occupant in each is progressively more Quentin — younger, older, sitting straighter. In the final photo the figure looks out of the frame. The beat is the past, present, and future collapsing into one image.

chapters.title: Love Against Duty
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Quentin and Odette fight over who sits in the chair; Quentin argues they're the nurse, trained to give comfort, so it's duty; Odette argues Quentin has more to lose, so it's love. Both are lying about their reasons. The beat is the theme argued in a kitchen at 3 a.m.

chapters.title: Four, Three
chapters.summary: Voss's POV. Voss reaches three and forgets his daughter, then his name, and walks into the frost toward the house, smiling. Quentin and Odette follow his trail of abandoned belongings like breadcrumbs in reverse. The beat is the cost of a life spent on duty, paid in full.

chapters.title: The Occupant Speaks
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. In the ritual room, the thing in the chair speaks with Quentin's voice and offers a bargain: sit down, keep your love, lose everything else — or walk away and let it finish with the town. Quentin realizes the occupant is every version of themself that ever considered believing. The beat is temptation with a familiar face.

chapters.title: Two
chapters.summary: Odette's POV. The frost reaches the doorstep and begins writing the final pattern across the floorboards of the whole house. Odette, who swore never to enter the ritual room, carries her brother's list of loved things to the thirteenth chair and reads it aloud as an anchor. The beat is fierce, stubborn tenderness.

chapters.title: The Ritual Finished
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Quentin sits in Zephyrine's chair not as a sacrifice but as a keeper — completing the founders' ritual the way Zephyrine intended, binding the thing to a living memory freely given rather than a life devoured. The room fills with every memory Quentin owns, offered one by one. The beat is transcendence inside terror; the counting stops at one.

chapters.title: One
chapters.summary: Odette's POV. The frost melts, the chair is gone, the photographs are ordinary — except one, in which Quentin stands beside the empty thirteenth chair, looking out. Quentin wakes in the kitchen knowing Odette's name and nothing else, and asks who she is. The beat is devastating quiet: the price paid, the person preserved.

chapters.title: What Remains
chapters.summary: Odette's POV, epilogue. Odette takes Quentin home to the city, keeping the list, the journals, and the one photograph in a shoebox she never explains. When Quentin, a hospice nurse again, hears a dying patient count backwards and feels only professional calm, Odette grips their hand — and Quentin, without knowing why, holds on. The beat is love outlasting memory: the answer to the book's question.
